editor_spans.body: The one concrete item in Andy Burnham's Motherwell speech cuts against a purely adversarial reading of his Scottish offer. Employment support run by the Department for Work and Pensions is reserved to Westminster. Offering a localised model 'shaped by Holyrood' hands Edinburgh something real. The condition is that the money must then go 'deep' to places, on the Easterhouse principle of 'names not numbers'. This is a trade, not just a bypass: a new power for the Scottish Government, in return for agreeing to pass it on. It gives John Swinney a harder choice than a flat refusal would.

Most of the rest is process. The diagnosis is vivid and specific: Ravenscraig, Leigh's pits, Dundee's empty shops, a seven-year life-expectancy gap. The remedies are things to 'design' in the coming months, powers to 'explore', and a National Economic Council meeting that has not happened before under this Prime Minister. Aberdeen is the place now living through deindustrialisation, as the North Sea winds down. It got one line and a promise of 'more to say in due course'. Ravenscraig is the speech's own example of a decision taken far away with no plan for afterwards. On that test, Aberdeen is where the new approach must prove itself first, and the speech left it empty.

The procurement pledge deserves more scrutiny than it will get. As mayor, Burnham paid more to buy Falkirk-built buses. He now wants all UK public procurement to work that way. That is a significant doctrine. It sits beside his push for closer EU ties and a food and farming deal in Brussels. A government seeking deeper alignment with Europe will find a 'buy British' procurement rule hard to defend at the same negotiating table. The extra cost of every contract won at home would also have to come from budgets already under pressure.
